Construction of the Studies Building and winterizing
The community begins building the Studies Building in fall 1940; winterizing of the existing buildings, a house for the cooks, farm buildings, and a cottage for Heinrich and Johanna Jalowetz.
Rice's final resignation

Before his final resignation, Rice had opposed the quest for economic security and physical permanence: communities, he said, should live from day to day; instability was their lifeblood. By 1940 he was only a peripheral figure, his carelessness in pronouncing maxims reducing his influence still further.

Rice resigns at the faculty's request: increasingly merciless criticism of colleagues and students; the failure of his friendship with a student to respect the subtle balance between intellect and emotions (his definition of intelligence); the frictions in his marriage, which had become a community problem.
Rice's fate after Black Mountain

Without a wife, money, or a job, with few friends and many regrets, Rice goes through bitter and lonely years, then recovers his spirits. He remarries, wins the Harper Prize for his autobiography, and then lives on occasional writing: a column for PM, stories for the New Yorker. According to his son, he mellowed a great deal in the last decade before his death in 1969.

Rice resigns from the faculty

In a brief memorandum dated February 17, 1940, Rice resigns from the faculty, effective at the end of the 1939-1940 year. After a last trip by Wunsch to Southern Pines, the financial arrangements for Rice and his family are settled, with a mutual promise to announce publicly only that he resigned of his own accord to devote himself to writing. Rice is devastated by a sense of terrible failure and terrible fate.
